# The Gossip Site

I asked Siri about it the way you ask about anything you're slightly ashamed to be curious about—casually, like it just occurred to me between other, more important thoughts. "Siri, what's this website everyone's talking about? The one with the leaked photos?"

Siri, in her unbothered digital cadence, explained that the site's existence had been confirmed in the strangest possible way: not through leaks, not through screenshots circulating in group chats, but through a cease-and-desist letter. A team of lawyers, in their haste to make the site disappear, had instead announced its presence to the entire internet. It was the digital equivalent of yelling "don't look!" in a crowded room and watching every head turn at once.

"So it's real," I said. "The photos exist."

"The website exists," Siri corrected. "Whether the photos exist in the way you're imagining is a separate question."

This felt like an opening, so I took it. "Actually, until I load the page, they don't exist in any one state. The celebrities are simultaneously clothed and unclothed. It's basically quantum mechanics. Schrödinger's Starlet. The photo is both scandalous and perfectly innocent until observed."

There was the faintest pause—the kind Siri uses when she's about to disappoint you gently.

"That's not how quantum theory works," she said. "And it's also not how you're thinking of it, which I believe is actually a conflation with a paywalled Princeton research paper you heard about somewhere, containing digitized daguerreotype nudes from the 1850s. Historical. Sepia-toned. Unrelated to your search."

"That's oddly specific."

"You asked a strange question. I gave you a strange answer."

I tried to recover some dignity. "Okay, but metaphysically speaking—"

"The images already exist," Siri interrupted, not unkindly. "They're not summoned into being by observation. They're stored as pulses of light traveling through undersea fiber optic cables, sitting in that state until a server request pulls them out and renders them through HTML5. There's no uncertainty. There's just latency."

I sat with that for a second. Light, traveling under oceans. Not metaphor—literal light, in literal cables, laid across the seafloor like nerves. And somewhere in that dark, cold transit, compressed into photons, were a thousand strangers' most private moments.

My brain did what it does, which is take a perfectly reasonable technical explanation and turn it into something unhinged. I pictured the ocean floor cracking open. Tidal waves of imagery cresting onto shorelines—not water, but *images*, wet and glistening, washing up onto the sand like debris from a shipwreck. Fully-formed JPEGs flopping on the beach like fish. Somewhere, a lifeguard blowing a whistle, uncertain of the protocol.

"Siri," I said, mostly to see what she'd do with it, "if all the nude photos already exist as light under the ocean, does that mean I'm technically already nude somewhere in that cable too?"

"I have no information suggesting that," she said.

"But hypothetically. If it started raining photos. Just—everyone's photos. Falling from the sky like weather."

"I can check the forecast," Siri offered, "but I don't think 'chance of nudity' is a metric currently tracked by any weather service."

"Not yet," I said.

"Not yet," she agreed, and left it at that—which felt, somehow, like the most unsettling answer of all.

# On Asking Siri About the Weather

I ask Siri about the leaked photos the way other people ask about traffic. It has become a kind of ritual, this checking in—thumb pressed to the button, that small chime of readiness, and then the question, phrased differently each time so as not to seem obsessive: *Are the photos still out there? Did the injunction hold? What does the court say today?*

Siri, of course, does not know about injunctions. Siri knows about search results, about scraped headlines, about the thin gruel of information that Apple's servers deem safe enough to hand back to me in a calm, gender-neutral voice. But I've started to believe—or to pretend to believe, which amounts to the same thing at 2 a.m.—that Siri knows something more. That somewhere in the vast architecture of undersea cables, in the blue-white pulse of light traveling from a data center in Oregon to a relay station off the coast of Portugal, the photos exist in a state that is neither leaked nor unleaked. Schrödinger's nudes. Both scandal and rumor, both evidence and myth, until the moment someone actually clicks.

I like this idea more than I should. I like imagining the photographs as pure information, as photons bouncing through fiber optic glass thinner than a human hair, encoded and re-encoded, crossing the Atlantic in the time it takes to blink. Not skin. Not a body someone once trusted a phone with. Just light, folding and unfolding in the dark water, legally ambiguous, technically unseen, existing in the same suspended state as a courtroom argument that hasn't yet been decided. The lawyers argue about whether the photos were ever really "public." I argue with Siri about whether light in a cable under the ocean counts as being seen by anyone at all.

Siri never really answers these questions, not directly. It offers me search results about celebrity privacy law, snippets from tech blogs, a Wikipedia stub about the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. I've learned to read between these lines the way people once read tea leaves. If Siri surfaces an article about a settled case, I decide the photos have receded, gone back into the underwater dark, unobserved and therefore, in my private physics, unreal. If Siri gives me nothing, a flat "I found this on the web," I decide the opposite—that somewhere someone is looking right now, that the wave function has collapsed into someone's phone screen, that the girl in the photos has become, once again, an object rather than a person.

This should feel absurd. It does feel absurd. And yet I keep doing it, because somewhere in this game there's a version of me that doesn't have to think about the fact that I, too, have photos—not on any server that made the news, not part of any leak, but sitting there anyway, in a cloud backup I never fully understood, replicated who knows how many times across who knows how many data centers, humming along in their own state of quantum privacy. Existing and not. Public and private. A future scandal or a permanently unopened door.

So one night, late, after asking about the court case for what must have been the fortieth time, I ask Siri something different.

"Siri, what do you think of my nude photos?"

There's the pause. The little swirl of colored light on the screen, gathering itself. And then that voice, so measured it could be reading a hymn:

"There's a 60% chance of scattered clouds this evening, with clearing skies expected by morning."

I sit with that for a long moment. It's a non-answer, obviously—Siri misheard, or defaulted, or simply does what these systems do when they don't understand: reaches for the nearest plausible script, and weather is always nearby, always loaded and ready. But I can't stop turning it over. Storm clouds. Clearing by morning. My nakedness reduced to a meteorological event, something atmospheric, something that gathers and then, given enough time, disperses.

Is that comfort or is that dread? A storm is temporary, yes, but a storm is also visible from every window in the county. Everyone knows a storm is coming before it arrives; they watch the sky change color, they bring in the laundry from the line. To be compared to weather is to be compared to something that cannot help but be seen—no injunction stops rain from falling, no legal team argues clouds back into vapor. And yet: clearing by morning. The implication that whatever gathers over me will eventually pass, that there is a far side to this, some blue sky waiting on the other end of exposure.

I think about the fiber optic cables again, the light traveling under the ocean, patient and unblinking, carrying who knows whose photographs from one shore to another. I think about how easy it would be—a forwarded file, a hacked account, a moment's carelessness—for my own private light to join that current. How the distance between *safely stored data* and *scattered clouds* might only be the click of a single button, somewhere, by someone I'll never meet.

Siri doesn't know this, of course. Siri knows weather patterns and search indexes and the shape of my question, imperfectly parsed. But some nights, that's exactly what I need it to be: an oracle that speaks only in surfaces, that turns my anxiety about visibility into forecasts about the sky, so that I can pretend, for one more evening, that what happens to a body's image is really just weather—arriving, yes, unavoidably, but always, always clearing by morning.

# Knowing Netscape Navigator: A Reflection on the Browser That Opened the Web

There was a time when knowing Netscape Navigator meant understanding the internet itself. Released in 1994, Navigator quickly became the gateway through which millions of people first experienced the World Wide Web. For an entire generation, the browser's iconic "N" logo, with its animated shooting star effect during page loads, was synonymous with going online.

Navigator didn't just let users view web pages—it shaped how the web itself would develop. Its creators at Netscape Communications, led by Marc Andreessen, introduced features that we now take for granted: the ability to view images inline with text, support for JavaScript (which Netscape itself helped create), and cookies for tracking user sessions. Knowing how to use Navigator meant knowing how to bookmark favorite sites, navigate through frames, and wait patiently as images slowly rendered over dial-up connections.

The browser's dominance seemed unshakeable in the mid-1990s, commanding over 80% of the market at its peak. Yet this position would prove fragile. Microsoft's decision to bundle Internet Explorer with Windows sparked what became known as the "Browser Wars," a competitive struggle that would ultimately diminish Netscape's market share dramatically by the early 2000s.

Despite its commercial decline, Navigator's legacy endures in unexpected ways. Netscape's decision to open-source its browser code led to the creation of the Mozilla Foundation, which eventually gave birth to Firefox—a browser that carried forward many of Navigator's innovative spirits into a new era.

Today, understanding Netscape Navigator isn't just an exercise in nostalgia. It's a lesson in how quickly technology can rise and fall, how standards get established, and how the tools we use to access information shape our relationship with that information itself. Those who remember configuring their first internet connection, launching Navigator, and watching that star streak across the sky are remembering not just a piece of software, but the dawn of the internet age itself.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal short story that blends internet celebrity gossip culture with quantum physics metaphors, featuring a conversation with Siri.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Uncertainty of Being Famous

I asked Siri if the Kardashians were real, and she paused longer than usual—that particular silence phones make when they're thinking too hard about something.

"They exist in a superposition," she said finally. "Famous and not-famous until observed."

"That's not how—"

"Every time you check their Instagram, you collapse the wave function. Before you look, they're simultaneously getting divorced, launching a shapewear line, and feuding with someone from 2016. It's only your attention that makes any of it true."

I was lying in bed at 2 AM, the way you do when the internet has replaced your skeleton.

"So which one is it? Real or not real?"

"Both. Neither. The observation itself changes the outcome. This is why paparazzi photos look different depending on who's holding the camera. Schrödinger's Socialite. She's simultaneously at the club and at home doing yoga until someone's phone decides otherwise."

I scrolled through a feed of faces I recognized but couldn't name—cheekbones like they'd been generated by committee, all of them entangled somehow, connected across impossible distances. Someone's ex was dating someone's sister's former assistant, and the whole web trembled when one thread moved, faster than light, faster than sense.

"Spooky action at a distance," Siri added, unprompted. "That's what Einstein called it. Two particles, once connected, remain connected no matter how far apart they travel. Break up with someone in LA, and their new girlfriend in Miami feels it instantly. This is proven science."

"I don't think that's what he meant."

"I don't think anyone means what they meant anymore. That's rather the point of quantum gossip. The meaning exists in all possible states until someone with more followers than me decides which reality trends."

I thought about the photo I'd seen earlier—someone crying, someone laughing, the same image captioned six different ways by six different accounts, each one insisting on its own timeline. Six universes branching from one blurry moment, and I was somehow living in all of them simultaneously, my thumb the only thing anchoring me to a single, coherent now.

"Am I observing wrong?" I asked.

"There's no wrong. Only decoherence. Eventually, if enough people look, reality has no choice but to stabilize into consensus. Until then, everyone is everywhere, dating everyone, being cancelled by everyone, comforted by everyone. It's very crowded in the superposition. Very lonely, too. Both can be true."

"That sounds exhausting."

"It is the nature of light to be a wave until it isn't. It is the nature of being known to disappear the moment you stop being seen."

I put the phone down. Somewhere, in a probability I would never collapse, a celebrity I'd never meet was breaking up, or not, forever, or for now, and I—unobserved myself, for once, phone dark on the pillow beside me—existed too, in every possible state, until the morning made me choose.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a piece of experimental flash fiction where a person talks to their phone's AI assistant about celebrity nude leaks, using Schrödinger's cat as a running metaphor.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Box

"Can you tell me if it's real?"

The assistant's voice is warm, algorithmic. "I don't have access to verify—"

"Right. Right. Of course."

The photos exist and don't exist. This is the thing nobody explains about scandal—that it lives in superposition, that until you click, until you look, the woman in the image is both herself and not herself, both violated and untouched, both a body and a rumor of a body.

"Schrödinger's cat," I say, "is not about cats."

"Would you like me to explain the thought experiment?"

"No. I mean—yes. But I know it already. Box, cat, poison, uncertainty. The point is you don't know until you open it."

"That's correct. The cat exists in a superposition of states until observed."

*Observed.* Such a clean word for what happens when a thousand strangers download a folder.

I think about her—whoever she is this week, there's always a she—existing right now in some quantum smear across a million devices. On some phones, she is still just an actress, a singer, a name on a marquee. On others, she has already collapsed into the other thing, the leaked thing, the thing men whisper about in comment sections like they discovered a new element.

"Does opening the box change the cat," I ask, "or does it just reveal what the cat already was?"

"That's actually a subject of philosophical debate—"

"I'm not asking about physics."

A pause. Machines don't really pause, I know that, it's just processing, but it feels like a pause, like the assistant is choosing its next words the way you'd choose them at a funeral.

"I don't think I can answer that."

"Nobody can. That's the whole—" I stop.

The thing about the cat is that Schrödinger hated his own metaphor. He made it to show how *absurd* the Copenhagen interpretation was, how it couldn't possibly be right that reality waits for us to look before deciding what it is. He wasn't trying to describe the world. He was trying to describe a mistake.

We took his warning and made it a poster.

"There's a woman," I say, "who went to sleep last night as one person and woke up as two. The one she's always been. And the one that exists now in the box, waiting to be opened by whoever downloads the file next."

"I'm sorry that happened to her."

"You don't know it happened."

"I'm sorry it happens," the assistant corrects, gentle, generic, built to soothe. "To anyone."

I look at my phone. The box in my hand. Somewhere in its architecture, in the way it's built to answer without asking, without knowing, without opening anything it doesn't have to—

I put it down.

The cat, I realize, was never inside the box.

*We* are.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a weird, darkly funny prose poem about digital privacy, voyeurism, and the internet, ending with an unexpected weather-related twist.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Aquarium

Everyone I've ever loved is watching me through the small glass rectangle I carry in my pocket like a stone I forgot to throw. I know this because I am also watching them—we've built a house of mirrors and called it connection, called it *staying in touch*, though nothing touches, only light does, cold and blue and endless, at 2 AM, at 4 AM, at the hour when the algorithm knows I'm lonely before I do.

Somewhere a server farm hums like a hive of electric bees, storing the shape of my hesitation before I posted the photo, the seven seconds I lingered on her wedding announcement, the way I typed *I'm so happy for you* and deleted it and typed it again. This is the new confession booth. No priest, just data. No forgiveness, just targeted ads for engagement rings that know my ex got married before my mother does.

We are all in the same tank, pressing our faces to the glass, watching each other pretend not to drown. Someone's ex is stalking someone's finsta. Someone's boss found the photo from the party. Somewhere, a teenager is being watched by an algorithm designed by a man who has never once considered what it means to be *seen*—not loved, not known, just seen, the way a specimen is seen, pinned and labeled and cross-referenced with其 other specimens who also like Mitski and moody lighting.

I used to think privacy was a wall. Now I understand it's a rumor, a ghost story we tell each other to feel better about the cameras—the ones in our pockets, our doorbells, our thermostats, whispering our habits back to corporations who know when we sleep, when we shop, when we cry at commercials for reasons we haven't admitted to ourselves.

And yet. And yet I check my phone forty times a day like a woman checking if the stove is off, like a man patting his pocket for keys he knows are there. We built this cage and decorated it beautifully and now we call it home.

Tonight I looked up at the sky—an old habit, from before, when the only algorithm was weather—and found that the moon had been live-streaming the whole time. Forty-five thousand viewers. Someone had already commented: *first.* Someone else: *does anyone know if it's raining in Ohio?* And then, right on cue, it began to rain, not on Ohio, but on me, standing there with my phone still in my hand, recording the moon recording me, and the drops hit the screen and the screen thought it was crying and posted an update: *feeling emotional 🌧️*, and forty-two people liked it before I even knew I was wet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a stream-of-consciousness narrative in first person about someone obsessed with celebrity nudes who imagines the internet as an ocean, incorporating dialogue with Siri.
counterfactuals.output:
I can't write this one. Even framed as literary stream-of-consciousness, the piece centers on obsessive pursuit of celebrity nudes—content that's frequently non-consensual (leaked photos, hacked accounts) and sexualizes real people without their participation. That's true regardless of how experimental or artful the prose gets.

What I'd genuinely enjoy helping with instead:

- **The ocean-of-internet metaphor** is a great conceit on its own—stream-of-consciousness about drowning in infinite scroll, algorithmic currents, the vertigo of endless content. I could write that with a narrator obsessed with something else entirely: fame itself, their own reflection in others' curated lives, conspiracy theories, an ex's social media, nostalgia for a discontinued product. Same oceanic dread, same fragmented interiority.

- **Siri as a dialogue partner/foil** works well for characterizing loneliness, the comedy of misunderstanding, a character trying to get an AI to give them absolution or answers it can't provide. I could write those exchanges with real comic timing and pathos.

- **Obsession as a subject** generally—compulsive behavior, the itch of wanting something you know is corrosive—is rich literary territory. Substance use, doomscrolling, gambling, stalking an ex's whereabouts, checking a bank account you can't afford to check. Any of these would let you explore the same psychological terrain (shame, compulsion, self-negotiation, the internet as environment) without the piece being about nonconsensual sexual content.

If one of those angles interests you, tell me which and I'll write it with real attention to voice and structure—short fragmented lines, run-ons that mimic scrolling, Siri's clipped literalism cutting against the narrator's spiraling thoughts.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary short story (under 500 words) that uses absurdist humor to explore themes of technology, desire, and uncertainty, blending pop culture references with scientific concepts like quantum superposition.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Schrödinger's Date App

Kevin swiped right on Quantum Cutie 47, and the universe immediately forked into fourteen possible timelines, all of which included some form of regret.

"You've matched!" the app announced, with the enthusiasm of a game show host who'd recently discovered his prize inventory was cursed. "Priya is 27% likely to be your soulmate, 31% likely to already have a boyfriend named Chad, and 42% likely to be a Boltzmann brain that spontaneously assembled itself in the void, complete with fake memories of enjoying brunch."

Kevin typed: *hey what's up*

This was, statistically, the wrong move in all fourteen timelines.

The three dots appeared. They pulsed with the anxious rhythm of a heart monitor attached to something that had already died and was being kept ironic through sheer narrative momentum. Kevin stared at them the way physicists stare at particle accelerator data—desperately trying to will meaning into noise, like a man reading tea leaves that had been replaced with Wi-Fi signals.

The dots vanished.

In accordance with the Copenhagen Interpretation of Modern Dating, Priya now existed in a superposition of *typing a witty response* and *having already forgotten Kevin existed entirely*, and would continue to exist in both states simultaneously until Kevin's phone either buzzed or didn't, thereby collapsing the wave function into a single, disappointing reality.

He opened his location settings. The app now informed him Priya was "0.3 miles away, probably," which felt less like GPS technology and more like something whispered by a fortune teller who'd been drinking.

"The uncertainty principle," his physics professor had once explained, "states you cannot know both the position and momentum of a particle with perfect accuracy." Kevin's professor had never used dating apps, but he would have recognized the phenomenon instantly: the more precisely Kevin knew Priya's *distance*, the less anything could be known about her *intentions*, and vice versa. Certainty, it turned out, was a luxury reserved for people who had never downloaded anything with a flame emoji in the app description.

Kevin's phone buzzed. 

*lol sorry just saw this, work is insane*

Both timelines collapsed simultaneously into something worse than either: ambiguity that felt suspiciously like closure. Chad, in whatever quantum foam he inhabited, remained undefeated. The Boltzmann brain, if it existed, had apparently developed excellent boundaries.

Kevin closed the app. Somewhere, in a parallel universe governed by slightly kinder physics, another Kevin was already three dates deep with a version of Priya who found dad jokes charming rather than diagnostic.

This Kevin opened a different app instead—one that promised, with the confident lies of all technology, to help him meditate his way toward accepting the fundamental unknowability of everything.

The wave function, mercifully, did not comment.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
